nodes.title: Dehumanization
nodes.text: Denying people their full humanity: treating them as objects, problems, threats or numbers, so that harming, controlling or erasing them starts to seem acceptable.

nodes.title: Indigenous Peoples
nodes.text: In Night, after getting deported, Eliezer loses his name and gets reduced to a number. Indigenous children who were sent to Canada’s residential schools also lost their names, languages and families. Indigenous authors such as Jenny Kay Dupuis tell these stories themselves instead of having others tell them.  In Dupuis’s I Am Not a Number, the story of her grandmother Irene, who was displaced from her family and had her name replaced with a number, shows this almost exactly as Wiesel describes it. It is a Canadian echo of Eliezer’s experience, told by an Indigenous author about her own family. Voices like hers matter to decolonize the literary world because they challenge who gets to define Indigenous history and whose stories are taught in classrooms.

nodes.title: Kamloops Indian Residential School
nodes.text:
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7-aEZFxA4bQ

I selected this CBC News video because it shows an Indigenous community announcing the truth about its own missing children. The Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation said preliminary findings from a survey of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School grounds uncovered the remains of 215 children. The bodies were found during a ground-penetrating radar survey; the children ranged in age, with the youngest being as little as three years old, and their deaths were undocumented. This supports my argument because it is the same process Eliezer goes through in Night, where an authority erases a person’s name and turns them into a number, and no one with power feels responsible for recording what happened. Just as Wiesel refuses to let that erasure stand, Indigenous communities and authors like Dupuis work to restore the names and stories of children that institutions left out. This video also matters for decolonizing the literary world because the discovery came from Indigenous people searching for their own missing children, which challenges who gets to define Indigenous history and whose stories are taught in classrooms.

nodes.title: I am not a number by Jenny Kay Dupuis
nodes.text: Based on a true story, I Am Not a Number follows eight-year-old Irene, a First Nations girl forced into a Canadian residential school where she is given the number 759 to erase her identity. Holding onto her heritage, she endures the school until returning home for the summer, where her parents hide her so she never has to go back.

nodes.title: Residential Schools
nodes.text: I selected this photo of Indigenous boys at a residential school because it shows exactly how institutions turned individual children into a group. The boys wear matching caps and jackets, and they are arranged in rows on the steps for the camera. Their faces look serious and their bodies stiff; the caption labels them only as a group of schoolboys, which is part of the point, since the record itself treats them as a category and not as individuals. This supports my argument because Eliezer goes through the same process in Night: he is shaved, put into a uniform, and given a number. In both cases, an authority decided that a person’s identity did not matter. The photograph also sets up my next point that Indigenous authors like Dupuis tell these stories themselves. In I Am Not a Number, she gives a name and a voice back to her grandmother Irene, who is one of the children this kind of photograph leaves nameless.

nodes.title: Black Canadians
nodes.text: Throughout Night, Wiesel displays moral exclusion in its most severe form: the act of placing a group outside the protection of human justice so that any harm done to them seems justified. When Eliezer arrives at Auschwitz, families are split apart with a single command; Eliezer talks about how babies were thrown into flaming pits, and that Dr. Mengele decided in seconds who would live and who wouldn't. No one with authority treated these people as members of a human community, so no one felt responsible for protecting them. Black Canadians have faced a similar kind of exclusion as well; an example of this is Africville, a Black community in Halifax that was denied basic services like paved roads and clean water, which then led to the community being demolished, with hundreds of civilians relocated. This is a clear reason why Black Canadian voices matter for decolonizing literature because by writing their own stories, they challenge whose experiences get taught.

nodes.title: UNESCO
nodes.text:
Link: https://www.instagram.com/p/Dbt3CPhoHB_/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&hvrq=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==

I selected this Instagram post from the Africville Museum because it shows Africville telling its own story. The post announces that in 2024, Africville was officially designated as Canada’s first UNESCO Place of History and Memory linked to Enslavement and the Slave Trade. The building in the photo is a replica of the Seaview United Baptist Church, which was the heart of Africville for generations. The original was lost when the community was demolished, so the rebuilt church is a form of reclaiming what was taken. The image places it in the center, under a bright sky, presenting the church as a symbol of survival and pride instead of loss. The museum itself is run by a board made up mostly of members of the Africville community; remarks in the caption like “our history” and “our community” matter because they come from the people the city once treated as expendable. This supports my argument because my photo of the Africville water source shows how the community was neglected, while this post shows the community reclaiming its story and having its history recognized around the world. This is the opposite of moral exclusion: a group that was once placed outside the community’s circle of fairness is now insisting on being remembered. It also connects to Night, because Wiesel’s repeated “Never shall I forget” (Wiesel 34) shows the same belief that remembering is a way of refusing erasure. The museum states that it will continue sharing its history and educating the public, which shows why Black Canadian voices matter to decolonize the literary world, as when communities tell their own stories, they challenge whose experiences get taught and remembered.

nodes.title: The struggles to maintain Africville
nodes.text: I selected this specific photo of Africville because it provides direct evidence of the unequal treatment I’m arguing about. The sign in the center reads, “Please boil this water before drinking and cooking,” and the water source behind it is a wooden box in an open field. This shows that a community inside Halifax, a major city, was expected to survive without safe running water. The houses in the background highlight the strong community that was persevering against these methods of exclusion and oppression. This highlights moral exclusion: when a group of people are placed outside the community’s circle of fairness, neglect starts to seem normal, and later even harm seems justified, as shown by the demolition and relocation of the community. This is the same process Wiesel demonstrates in Night, where people stop being treated as members of a human community and no one feels responsible for protecting one another. This photo also leads to my next point, because records like this show Africville only through its neglect, while Black Canadian authors tell their own stories and show the people and history better than a photo can.

nodes.title: Mental Health
nodes.text: Throughout the memoir, Wiesel shows that dehumanization does not end when the violence does, as it leaves traces of lasting psychological damage. Eliezer describes himself as “nothing but a body. Perhaps even less: a famished stomach" (Wiesel 52). This shows how starvation and fear reduced him to solely survival instinct. After his father dies of dysentery, he feels relief, and then nothing matters to him anymore. The same boy who cried during prayer can no longer cry at all; when he sees himself in the mirror after liberation, he sees a corpse, and the look in his eyes never leaves him. Using a mental health lens, the trauma, numbness and survivor’s guilt can be seen as real and lasting harm rather than just weakness, something readers are asked to recognize instead of just looking away from. Lindsay Wong continues this work in her memoir The Woo-Woo, where she writes about mental illness within her own family, a topic that is often hidden or dismissed. Like Wiesel, she tells her own story instead of having someone else explain it for her. Voices like theirs matter to aid in decolonizing the literary world because they challenge which experiences of suffering and recovery are taught and believed, and they make room for stories that have been silenced.

nodes.title: Night and Silence
nodes.text: Night exemplifies the long-lasting damage caused by dehumanization even after the violence stops, which supports my mental health argument. On his first night in Auschwitz, Eliezer watches a kapo strike his father and does nothing, and he asks himself, “Had I changed that much?” (Wiesel 39) Fear has already taught him to stay silent. At Buchenwald, as his father weakens, Eliezer is torn between caring for him and protecting his own strength, and once his father dies, relief is part of what he feels, followed by the numbness of feeling that nothing matters anymore. This is survivor’s guilt, shown in plain language instead of explained. The symbols of night and silence add to this; night represents death and despair, while Eliezer describes a silence from the world and from God that is all-consuming. Wiesel tells all of this plainly, like a report, which leaves readers to make their own judgments and asks them to recognize this suffering as real instead of looking away.

nodes.title: Buchenwald concentration camp
nodes.text: I selected this photo because it shows the cruel treatment of the victims of the Holocaust. We can see the victims malnourished, with bones sticking out, but also the number of people crammed into the wooden bunk. The photo treats them as a group, but their faces make them individuals, as several look directly at the viewer. This shows the physical side of the damage and highlights Eliezer’s description of himself as “a body” (Wiesel 52), making it easier to see what he was experiencing. This supports my argument because the starvation and overcrowding did not only harm their bodies. It led to the numbness Eliezer describes at the end of the memoir when he feels nothing after his father’s death and sees a corpse in the mirror. Through a mental health lens, this photo reminds readers that the suffering was real and that it explains why survivors have carried it long after liberation. It also reminds readers that Wiesel wrote this story himself, so the suffering is told by someone who actually lived it instead of it being explained by someone else.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.text: Elie Wiesel’s Night is a memoir about a boy who is stripped of his name, his family, and his faith by people who decide he does not belong to the human community. Canada was not the site of the Holocaust, but it was not innocent either. In 1939, the MS St. Louis, carrying 907 Jewish refugees, was denied entry to Canada, and 254 of its passengers later died in the Holocaust. Between 1933 and 1945, Canada admitted fewer than 5,000 Jewish refugees under what is known as the “none is too many” policy, and in 2018 the Prime Minister formally apologized for it. This history shows that the ideas behind moral exclusion, treating a group as unworthy of protection, also shaped Canadian policy. Night connects to this as it shows how devastating the Holocaust was, and the fate of the St. Louis passengers shows what exclusion cost when countries like Canada closed their doors. My three lenses show how that exclusion looked in different communities and why their own voices matter. This is shown through Canada's history with Indigenous children in residential schools, the Black community of Africville and the lasting psychological harm that survivors carry. Therefore, through an examination of Indigenous, Black Canadian, and mental health voices in Night, by Elie Wiesel, the reader achieves a heightened understanding of the importance of decolonizing the literary world.

nodes.title: The Woo-Woo: How I Survived Ice Hockey, Drug Raids, Demons, and My Crazy Chinese Family By Lindsay Wong
nodes.text: Set largely in Vancouver, the book follows Wong's upbrining with a grandmother who had paranoid schizophrenia and a mother who attributed psychological distress and crises to chinese ghosts and demons rather than seeking psychiatric care.

nodes.title: Reasoning
nodes.text: Night is the strongest text for my Mental Health argument, as it is a first-person account written by someone who lived through it. Wiesel does not have anyone else explain his experience for him, and that is the heart of my thesis about decolonizing the literary world. I selected Lindsay Wong’s memoir The Woo Woo because, like Night, it is a first-person memoir written by someone who lived what she describes. It is also a Canadian memoir about mental illness within her own family, a topic that's often hidden or dismissed. One specific example would be how Wong’s family believed mental illness was caused by demonic possession, which meant it was not treated. This connects to my analysis of Night, where Eliezer describes a silence from the world and from God that leaves him alone. In both memoirs, suffering gets worse when it is not acknowledged, and both writers refuse to let others explain their experiences for them. This supports my thesis that decolonizing the literary world means making room for the people who lived these stories to tell them.

nodes.title: Moral Exclusion
nodes.text: a psychological process in which individuals or groups place others outside their "moral community," viewing them as undeserving of fairness, compassion, or justice. Because excluded targets are seen as expendable or outside moral rules, harming, ignoring, or exploiting them can feel justified or acceptable to the group.

nodes.title: Night by Elie Wiesel
nodes.text: Elie Wiesel’s memoir Night traces how systematic dehumanization strips prisoners of their names, dignity, faith, and human solidarity inside Nazi concentration camps. Through first-person testimony, Wiesel shows how violence, starvation, and indifference push people toward survival at the expense of moral bonds, while silence from the outside world enables cruelty to continue. Bearing witness becomes a way to resist erasure and preserve memory so the suffering of victims is neither forgotten nor repeated. Connecting Night to other marginalized voices highlights why centering lived experiences is essential to challenging dominant narratives and decolonizing literature.

nodes.title: Africville
nodes.text: Africville was a historic Black community near Halifax, Nova Scotia, established in the 19th century by Black settlers and formerly enslaved people. Despite paying taxes, residents faced decades of municipal neglect, including a lack of basic infrastructure like paved roads, running water, and sewers, while city-approved industrial sites and dumps were placed nearby. In the 1960s, Halifax officials expropriated the land, demolished homes, and dispersed the residents under the banner of urban renewal. Today, Africville is remembered for its strong community bond and ongoing advocacy for justice, including formal apologies, compensation, and recognition as a historic site.
